chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Emerging Market Crises of the 1990s

lessons.title: The 1997 Asian Financial Crisis: Thailand, Korea, and the IMF

body.text: A fixed exchange rate makes borrowing in dollars look free of currency risk. That illusion lasts exactly until the peg breaks, and then every dollar loan in the country becomes more expensive on the same day.

children.text: On 2 July 1997, the Bank of Thailand gave up. For months it had defended the baht's value of about 25 per US dollar, committing about $24 billion of its reserves to the fight, much of it through forward currency contracts. By the time it let the currency float, only about $2.85 billion of usable reserves remained. By January 1998, a dollar cost 56 baht.

Within six months, the crisis had spread from Bangkok to Manila, Jakarta, Kuala Lumpur, Hong Kong and Seoul. Economies the World Bank had celebrated as the "East Asian miracle" needed IMF rescues. India, just six years after its own crisis, came through almost untouched. This lesson explains both outcomes.

stats.label: Indonesian rupiah per US dollar
stats.context: Dollar debts became seven times heavier

body.caption: The Asian crisis on the five-stage map

cells: Build-up
Fast-growing economies with currencies pegged or tightly managed against the dollar borrow heavily in short-term foreign currency, much of it for property and speculative projects
Trigger
Thailand's property and finance company bust, and speculative attacks that drain the Bank of Thailand's reserves
Panic and recognition
The baht floats on 2 July 1997; foreign lenders pull back from every similar economy in the region
Policy response
IMF-led packages for Thailand, Indonesia and Korea with tough conditions; Malaysia chooses capital controls instead
Repair and recovery
Bank clean-ups, corporate restructuring and huge reserve build-ups; most economies grow again by 1999, Indonesia more slowly

children.text: Build-up: The Miracle and the Mismatch

Through the early 1990s, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia and South Korea grew at spectacular rates. Foreign money poured in. Their currencies were pegged or tightly managed against the US dollar, so local banks and companies saw no reason to fear borrowing in dollars. Dollar interest rates were lower than local ones, which made the trade look even better.
That trade is a
carry trade
. It created a dangerous
currency mismatch
across entire economies: debts in dollars, income in baht, rupiah or won.

markDefs.definition: Borrowing in a currency with low interest rates to invest in assets or loans in a currency with higher interest rates, pocketing the difference. It is profitable only as long as the exchange rate stays stable.

When a borrower's debts are in one currency, typically US dollars, while its income or assets are in another, typically the local currency. A fall in the local currency increases the debt burden without any new borrowing.

body.text: The peg did not remove currency risk. It hid it and concentrated it. Every company that skipped hedging because "the rate never moves" was making the same bet, so when the peg broke, they all lost at once.

children.text: Worse, much of the borrowing was short-term. In Thailand, Indonesia and Korea, short-term foreign debt exceeded available forex reserves just before the crisis. You met this warning sign in the India 1991 lesson. Here it appeared across a whole region.

body.title: The Rupiah Debt Multiplier
body.prompt: An Indonesian property developer borrowed $1 million when the rupiah was at 2,400 per dollar. Its income is entirely in rupiah. When the rupiah falls to 16,800 per dollar, how many times larger is the debt measured in rupiah?
body.explanation: At 2,400, the debt is 2.4 billion rupiah. At 16,800, the same $1 million is 16.8 billion rupiah. 16,800 ÷ 2,400 = 7. The debt became seven times heavier in the currency the developer actually earns, without it borrowing one more dollar. Multiply that across thousands of companies and banks, and the whole corporate sector becomes insolvent.

children.text: Trigger: Thailand Cracks

Thailand's boom had flowed heavily into property, funded by lightly regulated finance companies that borrowed abroad. When property prices turned, their loans went bad. The Thai authorities suspended 16 finance companies on 27 June 1997 and a further 42 on 5 August, and 58 were eventually shut down, including Finance One, once the country's largest finance company.
Currency speculators saw that Thailand could not defend its peg forever and bet heavily against the baht. The Bank of Thailand fought back, but it was fighting with a finite pile of dollars.

body.title: Go deeper: how a speculative attack on a peg works

children.text: A peg is a promise by the central bank to buy its own currency at a fixed price, using its dollar reserves. A speculative attack is a bet that the promise will run out.
Speculators borrow baht, or agree to sell baht in the future, and convert them into dollars at the pegged rate of 25.
To hold the peg, the central bank must buy those baht, paying out dollars from its reserves.
Every dollar paid out makes reserves smaller and the peg less credible, attracting more speculators.
If the central bank gives up and the baht falls to 50, speculators buy back the baht they owe at half the price and keep the difference.

The bet is lopsided. If the peg holds, speculators lose only a little in interest costs. If it breaks, they win big. That is why attacks tend to get stronger, not weaker, as reserves shrink. The Bank of Thailand used $24 billion before it finally let the baht go.
Panic and Contagion: From Bangkok to Seoul

events.title: Thailand suspends 16 finance companies
events.description: Stress in the property-linked finance sector becomes impossible to hide.

events.title: The baht floats
events.description: After spending two thirds of its reserves, the Bank of Thailand abandons the peg. The crisis officially begins.

events.title: The Philippines lets the peso float
events.description: The first domino outside Thailand falls within ten days.

events.title: Indonesia floats the rupiah
events.description: Indonesia abandons the rupiah's trading band. The same month, Thailand accepts an IMF-led package of about $17 billion.

events.title: Hong Kong shares crash
events.description: The Hang Seng falls 10.4% in a day after banks' lending rates are pushed up sharply to defend the Hong Kong dollar's peg.

events.title: Indonesia closes 16 banks
events.description: Under its IMF programme, Indonesia shuts 16 banks with only partial deposit guarantees. Depositors run on the rest of the banking system.

events.title: Korea's record rescue
events.description: The IMF agrees to a $58 billion package for South Korea, one of Asia's largest economies.

events.title: The won hits bottom
events.description: The Korean won reaches 1,960 per dollar, from about 813 at the end of June.

events.title: Korea's gold collection campaign
events.description: About 3.5 million citizens donate jewellery and heirlooms, collecting around 227 tonnes of gold to help repay the country's foreign debt.

events.title: Suharto resigns
events.description: After riots and economic collapse, Indonesia's president steps down after 32 years in power.

events.title: Malaysia imposes capital controls
events.description: Malaysia rejects the IMF route, restricts money leaving the country and pegs the ringgit at 3.80 per dollar.

body.title: Value each currency lost against the US dollar at its worst point in the crisis

children.text: The Indian rupee bar is not a mistake. Across 1997-98, the rupee traded between ₹35.45 and ₹39.49 per dollar, a loss of about 10% of its value at the extreme, compared with more than half for the baht and won, and more than 85% for the rupiah.
The real economy took the hit next. In 1998, Indonesia's economy shrank by about 13%, and Thailand's by more than 10%. Korea and Malaysia also fell into deep recessions.

body.title: Why Closing Banks Caused a Run
body.question: On 1 November 1997, Indonesia closed 16 weak banks as part of its IMF programme, guaranteeing deposits only up to a limit. Instead of calming the system, it triggered runs on other banks. Why?
options: Depositors were relieved and moved money into the closed banks
Depositors could not tell which bank would be closed next, and large deposits were not protected, so they pulled money from banks across the system
The closed banks were the country's strongest banks
The IMF froze all bank deposits in Indonesia
body.explanation: This is Chapter 1's confidence problem. Closing some banks without a full guarantee told depositors that banks could fail and that big deposits might be lost, but not which banks were next. The safest move for any depositor was to withdraw first. Indonesia later had to introduce a blanket guarantee to stop the runs. Compare that with the US deposit insurance of 1934, which worked precisely because it removed the reason to run.

children.text: The IMF's Medicine, and the Argument About It
The IMF lent large sums to Thailand, Indonesia and Korea, but with strict conditions attached. It was one of the most debated rescues in the Fund's history.

body.title: The IMF's approach vs its critics

columns.label: The IMF's reasoning
points: Raise interest rates to stop currencies collapsing further
Close or restructure insolvent banks and finance companies quickly
Tighten government budgets to restore investor confidence
Demand structural reforms, such as ending cosy links between governments, banks and business groups

columns.label: The critics' objections
points: Very high interest rates bankrupted companies already crushed by dollar debts
Closing banks without full guarantees triggered runs, as in Indonesia
Budget cuts deepened recessions caused by a private debt problem, not government overspending
Too many conditions went beyond fixing the immediate crisis

body.label: Malaysia's Different Path
body.value: Capital controls and a peg at 3.80 ringgit per dollar
body.context: From 1 September 1998, Malaysia stopped offshore trading of the ringgit and barred portfolio investors from taking their money out for a year, while leaving trade and direct investment free. Economists still debate how much it helped, but it showed there was more than one policy response.

body.text: Compare Korea in 1998 with India in 1991. Both turned to gold in a foreign currency emergency. India's central bank pledged 46.91 tonnes as collateral. In Korea, about 3.5 million ordinary citizens donated around 227 tonnes of their own. Gold remains the asset of last resort in both cultures.

children.text: Why India Escaped
India entered 1997 with much of the same growth story that attracted money to East Asia, but with a very different balance sheet. Much of that difference came directly from the lessons of 1991.

body.caption: India vs the crisis economies in 1997

cells: Short-term foreign debt
Exceeded forex reserves
Low, a direct legacy of the 1991 crisis
Capital account
Largely open to foreign borrowing and hot money
Controlled; the rupee was convertible only for current transactions
Exchange rate
Pegged or tightly managed, so dollar borrowing looked riskless
Market-determined since 1993, with RBI smoothing volatility
Banks and property
Heavy lending to property funded by foreign borrowing
Very little bank exposure to real estate
Corporate debt
Heavily leveraged companies with dollar debts
Manufacturing debt to equity ratios had fallen from over 200% in 1991-92 to 121% by 1997-98

children.text: India did feel pressure. The rupee weakened and the RBI intervened in currency markets. In December 1997 and January 1998, it raised the cash reserve ratio and, in mid-January, increased the bank rate by 2 percentage points to make speculating against the rupee expensive. The pressure passed without a crisis.

body.label: A Reform Put on Hold
body.context: Weeks before the crisis, an RBI-appointed committee chaired by former Deputy Governor S.S. Tarapore laid out a roadmap to full capital account convertibility, subject to preconditions. After watching open capital accounts spread the Asian crisis, India put the plan on hold. The rupee is still not fully convertible on the capital account today.

body.title: Name the Weakness
body.textWithBlank: When a company earns in rupiah but owes its lenders in US dollars, it has a currency ___.
body.explanation: A currency mismatch. It was the single most destructive feature of the Asian crisis, because falling currencies turned millions of individually reasonable loans into unpayable ones at the same moment.

body.title: Spot the Next Thailand
body.scenario: Imagine an emerging economy today. It has grown at 7% a year for a decade. Its currency has been held within 1% of the dollar for eight years. Short-term foreign debt is 150% of its forex reserves. Its banks fund property loans partly with dollar deposits, and local developers prefer dollar loans because the rate is 4 percentage points cheaper. Its stock market is up 60% in two years, driven by foreign portfolio money.
body.prompt: List the 1997-style warning signs you can see, and explain what would most likely trigger a crisis and how it would spread.
body.modelAnswer: Warning signs: first, a rigidly managed currency that encourages borrowers to ignore currency risk. Second, short-term foreign debt at 150% of reserves, so the central bank cannot cover even one year of maturing debt if lenders refuse to roll over, the same weakness as Thailand, Indonesia and Korea. Third, a system-wide currency mismatch: dollar-funded property loans and dollar borrowing by developers who earn local currency, attracted by a carry trade. Fourth, a property and stock market boom fuelled by foreign portfolio money, which can leave quickly. Likely trigger: a property slowdown that exposes bad loans, a rise in US interest rates that pulls money home, or a crisis in a similar economy that sets off the wake-up call channel. How it spreads: foreign investors sell, the central bank spends reserves defending the currency, speculators sense the limit and attack. Once the currency breaks, dollar debts balloon in local terms, developers default, banks with dollar funding become insolvent, and the currency crisis becomes a banking crisis, the twin crisis pattern from Chapter 1. Neighbours with similar profiles would then face the same pressure.

cards.definition: Debts in a foreign currency, income in the local currency. A currency fall raises the debt burden instantly.
Borrowing cheaply in one currency to invest in higher-yielding assets in another, safe only while exchange rates stay stable.
Heavy betting against a pegged currency, draining the central bank's reserves until it can no longer defend the peg.
Policy conditions, such as higher rates, bank closures and budget cuts, attached to IMF rescue loans.
Limits on money moving in or out of a country, like those Malaysia imposed on 1 September 1998.
Freedom to convert local currency for investment and borrowing abroad. India shelved its plan after the Asian crisis.

points: Pegged currencies encouraged East Asian banks and companies to borrow short-term in dollars, creating a region-wide currency mismatch
Thailand spent $24 billion defending the baht before floating it on 2 July 1997; the baht fell from 25 to 56 per dollar by January 1998
Contagion spread to the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, Hong Kong and Korea, and the rupiah lost more than 85% of its value at its worst
IMF-led rescues for Thailand, Indonesia and Korea came with tough conditions that remain debated; Malaysia chose capital controls instead
India escaped because the lessons of 1991 had left it with low short-term debt, a controlled capital account, a flexible rupee and banks with little property exposure

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. The rupiah debt exercise and the emerging economy scenario are hypothetical illustrations. Historical figures are drawn from central bank, IMF, US government and other public sources, and some crisis statistics vary between sources.
